nodes.text: For unfailing predictions of earthquakes are recorded of him, and swift averting of plagues, and stillings of violent winds and of downpours of hail, and calmings of the waves of rivers and seas for the easy crossing of his companions. [They say that] Empedocles, Epimenides and Abaris, having had a share in these [powers], accomplished such things in many places; and their poems are plain evidence of it. Besides, Empedocles’ surname was ‘Wind-Averter’, Epimenides’ was ‘Purifier’, and Abaris’ was ‘Sky-Walker’, because, riding on an arrow of Apollo of the Hyperboreans that had been given to him, he crossed rivers and seas and trackless places, walking on the air, in a manner of speaking. Some supposed that Pythagoras too had experienced this when he conversed with his companions in Metapontum and in Tauromenium, in each place, on the same day.

He loved his friends exceedingly, being the first to declare that the possessions of friends are common, and that a friend is another self. When they were healthy he always spent time with them; when they were sick in body he tended them; and when they were sick in soul he consoled them, as we have said, some with incantations and magic, others with music. For he had songs that were healing even against diseases of the body, by chanting which he raised up the sick. And there were [songs] that produced forgetfulness of grief, soothed anger and removed improper desires.
